It cannot pass over from words ("I am a word junky, a word disease") to the supra or non verbal, the purely conceptual (and non-verbal: absolute abstraction). The paradoxes are obscured to her, despite Barefoot's best efforts (i.e., "the foolish come for the words; the wise eat the sandwich"). The Bishop is a topic in this novel only insofar as he holds out the gift of Divine foolishness to her, which she, in her rationality, rejects (at the end). _She_ is the real topic. But the Bishop offers the cure and solution, which she rejects; yet she comes so close! …

mention_cards.citation: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick, ed. Jackson & Lethem (2011), folio [90:6A]
mention_cards.context: Not Dick but his editors. The glossary appended to the 2011 Jackson and Lethem edition gives Burroughs a headword between Buber and Calvin, identifies him as an experimental Beat writer with his dates, and states the connection more confidently than Dick ever does: that Burroughs's notions of reality as a control system and of language as an extraterrestrial virus clearly resonated with him. It then supplies the one piece of chronology that exists nowhere else in the archive — that in 1978 Dick experimented with the cut-up method, which the glossary credits to Brion Gysin and attributes to Burroughs in use. Sutin describes that experiment without dating it, so this sentence is the only dating available. Two cautions belong with it. The confidence of clearly resonated should be read against Dick's own careful formulation that he and Burroughs sharply disagree; and the same sentence calls Gysin Swiss, when he was born in Taplow and held British and Canadian nationality.
mention_cards.pith: Burroughs's notions of reality as a control system and language as an extraterrestrial virus clearly resonated with Dick, who, in 1978, experimented with the cut-up method
mention_cards.speaker: Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem, eds.
mention_cards.editorial_note: The published edition’s own glossary. It dates Dick’s cut-up experiment to 1978, which Sutin leaves undated — the only dating of that experiment in the archive. Note an error in the same sentence: Gysin was British-Canadian, born in Taplow, not Swiss. Editorial apparatus, so register C, not Dick’s words.
mention_cards.passage: … **Burroughs, William S** . (1914–1997): Experimental Beat writer. Burroughs's notions of reality as a control system and language as an extraterrestrial virus clearly resonated with Dick, who, in 1978, experimented with the cut-up method developed by Swiss artist Brion Gysin and deployed by Burroughs. **Calvin, John** (1509–1564): French Protestant theologian. In the Exegesis, Calvin appears primarily as a proponent of the idea that prelapsarian human beings had extraordinary …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Bill Sarill, January 12, 1976 — Selected Letters 1975–1976
mention_cards.context: The earliest Burroughs reference in the archive, and it is about business rather than ideas — eight months before Dick reads him. Writing to his friend Bill Sarill, Dick describes being abruptly out of his little pond and into the big ocean: Doubleday's editors are enthusiastic enough about A Scanner Darkly to run off Xerox copies of the manuscript and send them to prominent American literary figures known to college readers, whose comments would go on the jacket. The names they want are Burroughs and Vonnegut and the other counterculture cult heroes. The rub, as he puts it, is that the approaches are left to him and he does not know any of them at all — the only people he knows are other science-fiction writers, and Doubleday does not want the novel read by anyone in science fiction, since they do not intend to market it that way. He notes that Ballantine, which is expected to take the paperback rights, does intend to market it as science fiction, but that is two years off.
mention_cards.pith: They want people like William Burroughs, Kurt Vonnegut—all the counterculture cult heroes to read it.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Earliest dated Burroughs reference found in the archive. Note that it is about publishing, not ideas: eight months before Dick reads him.
mention_cards.passage: … The problem is that now I am abruptly out of my little pond and into the big ocean, if you see what I mean. They—the Doubleday editors—are so enthusiastic about SCANNER that they intend to run off Xerox copies of the MS (no shit), and get prominent American literary figures known to the college people to read them and respond with comments, which I guess Doubleday will use on the back dj cover. They want people like William Burroughs, Kurt Vonnegut—all the counterculture cult heroes to read it. BUT, and here is the rub: it is up to me to approach such people, these literary greats, and in point of fact I don’t know any of them at all. Only people I know are other s-f writers. Doubleday doesn’t want the novel read by anyone in s-f. They are just not going to market it that way, although Ballant­ ine, which evidently is going to get paperback rights, intends to market it as s- f...which is another …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Sharon Jarvis, January 12, 1976 — Selected Letters 1975–1976
mention_cards.context: The same problem put to his agent on the same day, and the origin of a comparison that outlived him. Unable to reach the writers Doubleday wants, Dick falls back on what he can supply — review quotations about himself and his work in general — and lists his best: Oui, Tom Disch in Crawdaddy, Tony Hiss in the New Yorker. The line he copies out from Oui is the one that matters here: that in many ways Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs is to hard drugs and mainstream literature, and that he attracts students of the mind and unravellers of reality puzzles. The comparison is the magazine's, not Dick's. He then wonders whether Paul Williams might be able to link him up with Burroughs or Vonnegut or both, or come up with other names, and adds that the subject is not closed. The letter drifts on to whether quotations from the rock world would help, and to a go-between who might reach Grace Slick.
mention_cards.pith: In many ways, Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs is to hard drugs and mainstream literature.
mention_cards.speaker: Oui, quoted by PKD
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick quoting a review in Oui. The comparison is the magazine’s, not his.
mention_cards.passage: … to depend on is review quotes about me and my writing _in general._ I’ve got some good review quotes from _Oui,_ from Tom Disch writing in _Crawdaddy,_ from Tony Hiss writing in the New _Yorker._ For instance, _Oui_ says at one point: “In many ways, Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs is to hard drugs and mainstream literature. He attracts students of the mind and unravelers of reality puzzles,” etc. It’s possible that Paul Williams can link us up with either Burroughs or Vonnegut, or maybe both, or have some entirely original ideas of his own as to who to sound out. So the subject isn’t closed yet, as to what I (and Paul) can come up with. You want quotes from anyone in the rock scene? I’ve got …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Kate Wenner, Rolling Stone College Papers, October 5, 1979 — Selected Letters 1977–1979
mention_cards.context: A short, warm letter to Kate Wenner at Rolling Stone College Papers, thanking her for the first issue, which carried Dick's story Strange Memories of Death. He calls the issue stunning. What he singles out is the Burroughs material — an article followed by an interview — which he finds fascinating, and he notices that the interview leads directly into his own story, because Burroughs is discussing the rebellion of the Fifties and the Beats. The clause that follows is the reason this card exists: of which I was one. It is the only place in the archive where Dick claims the Beat affiliation for himself, and he does it in passing, as an observation about how well two pieces of magazine copy sit together. He goes on to praise the two-page illustration for his story, calling it among the best graphics he has ever had for a piece of his work, and says the artist caught the spirit of the story exactly.
mention_cards.pith: his interview leads right into my story inasmuch as he discusses the rebellion during the Fifties and the Beats, of which I was one.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Thank you for having a copy sent to me. The material on William Burroughs—the article and then the interview—is/are fascinating, and his interview leads right into my story inasmuch as he discusses the rebellion during the Fifties and the Beats, of which I was one. What especially pleased me was the two page illo for my story; it is the best, or one of the best, graphics I’ve ever had in connection with a piece of my work. And the artist absolutely caught …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Ben Adams, January 20, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Advice to a beginning writer named Ben Adams, and a rare direct statement of whom Dick thought worth reading. The counsel is practical and numbered. Write about what you actually know, and do not ignore the drama in ordinary lives, because there is drama in the most ordinary human life. Second, read the great prose writers — and the list is short, entirely outside science fiction, and includes Burroughs: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs, Saul Bellow, Herbert Gold. You cannot write if you have not read. Third, keep a journal of observations, overheard speech, reactions and thoughts. Fourth, pay little attention to negative criticism, since everyone fancies himself a critic; go on your own instincts, put a piece away for a week and see how you like it. He ends by telling Adams to hang in there, that writing is a lot of fun and also a lot of work, and that he will need luck.
mention_cards.pith: read the great prose writers: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs, Saul Bellow, Herbert Gold.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Don’t ignore the possibilities of drama in your life and the lives of those around you; there’s drama in the most “ordinary” human life. Second, read the great prose writ­ ers: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs, Saul Bellow, Herbert Gold. You can’t write if you haven’t read. Third, keep a journal; note down your observations, what you see, what you hear people say, your reaction to events, your thoughts. Fourth, don’t pay too much attention to negative criticism. Everyone fancies himself a critic. Go on …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Richard E. Geis, February 20, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Written to the fanzine editor Richard E. Geis while Dick was defending VALIS against the charge of being merely autobiography. He begins with the technical problem the first person creates, and takes it through Henry Miller — readers ask who this I is, and Miller's answer was, me, Henry Miller. Dick says he is greatly influenced by Miller, and that he chose to blur the distinction between himself and Horselover Fat, which is the penalty an author pays for writing in the first person. Then the statement of intention that names Burroughs: his purpose was a new kind of prose, a new blending of the ancient picaresque form with modern elements associated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs, and with his own 1977 novel A Scanner Darkly, which came out of his experiences in the drug subculture. The letter then turns to a related denial addressed to Ursula K. Le Guin — that the protagonist of Scanner is an undercover narcotics agent and he was not that either, which would have saved him a great deal of trouble.
mention_cards.pith: a new kind of blending of the ancient picaresque form with certain modern elements associated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Henry Miller discussed this problem, years ago. “Who is this T ?” readers ask. Miller’s answer was, “Me. Henry Miller.” I am greatly influenced by Henry Miller, but _my_ purpose was to achieve a new kind of prose, a new kind of blending of the ancient picaresque form with certain modern elements associ­ ated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs, as well as my own 1977 novel A SCANNER DARKLY based on my experiences with the drug subculture. Now, in A SCANNER DARKLY the protagonist is an undercover narcotics agent. I’m sorry, Ursula; I wasn’t that either. It would have saved me a lot of anxiety and trouble …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, February 23, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Three days after the Geis letter, the same account of VALIS is given to the scholar Patricia Warrick, with the politics attached. Dick has been describing his conflict with Ursula K. Le Guin, which he traces back to his earlier conflict with Lem, and his own position on the Soviet Union and its labour camps. He then characterises his preoccupations as not socially productive, comparing them to modern non-objective art — and the parallel he draws is that his writing is protest art pitted against official, formal culture, which is what the vernacular in VALIS is for. The Burroughs debt follows in one sentence: the book is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs, Hunter S. Thompson and his own A Scanner Darkly. He then describes what the novel is about — madness and God, told by a madman with whom he identifies himself not only as a character but ideologically and spiritually — and insists the madman's quest is valid, important and worthy of emulation.
mention_cards.pith: It is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs, Hunter S. Thompson
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … My preoccupations are not socially productive; they are like modem nonobjective art. In fact there is a decided parallel, because my writing is protest art pitted against official culture, formal culture. Hence my use of the ver­ nacular in VALIS. It is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs, Hunter S. Thompson and my own earlier novel, A SCAN­ NER DARKLY. VALIS is a novel about madness and God, told by a madman with whom I identify myself, not only as a character but (and this is far more important) ideologically and spiritually; I say that his quest, his goals, his journey, are valid and important and worthy and should be emulated. What is he seeking? He is seeking answers to …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: The opening of the most important document in the dossier: Dick's reply to a correspondent named Brig Elliot, written on 15 April 1981, one day before the Exegesis entry that states the reversal. He calls Elliot's letter fascinating and greatly appreciated. He then confirms what he has read, naming The Ticket That Exploded, and what he takes from it — the theory of an information virus, and with it the concept of latent information riding our ostensible traffic. The sentence that follows is the strongest single piece of evidence about the chronology of the whole relationship: back in 1971, before he knew of Burroughs, he had noticed a thinking dysfunction or occlusion in people involved with drugs, and he deals with it in A Scanner Darkly. He describes the dysfunction as puzzling and uneven, gross in some people and subtle in others, and gives the explanation he had reached at the time — that they were getting trace amounts of heavy metal in the drugs they used, which he notes certainly collates with Burroughs.
mention_cards.pith: Back in 1971 before I knew of Burroughs I noted a thinking dysfunction or occlusion in people involved with drugs; I deal with this in A SCANNER DARKLY.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dated one day before the Exegesis entry that states the reversal. Dick also dates his own observation of occlusion to 1971, "before I knew of Burroughs".
mention_cards.passage: … Yes, to a degree I am familiar with William Burroughs’ writing (e.g. TEIE TICKET THAT EXPLODED); I am familiar with his theory of an information virus. And, in respect to that, the concept of latent information riding our ostensible traf­ fic. Back in 1971 before I knew of Burroughs I noted a thinking dysfunction or occlusion in people involved with drugs; I deal with this in A SCANNER DARKLY. This dysfunction puzzled me. In some people it was gross, in others subtle. After research I came to the conclusion that these people were getting trace amounts of heavy metal in the drugs they used—which certainly collates …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: The fairest thing Dick ever wrote about someone he disagreed with, and it arrives out of a genuinely difficult observation. He has been describing a thinking dysfunction that goes unnoticed, especially by the people who have it, and identifying the horrifying part of it — that the self- monitoring circuit is fooled by the very dysfunction it is supposed to monitor, so that perhaps the monitor is itself malfunctioning. He notes he sees the same thing in himself, which is why Horselover Fat is identified as insane, and that superimposing A Scanner Darkly on VALIS yields the claim that the dysfunction is ubiquitous. Then the assessment. He cannot accept Burroughs's view that we have been invaded by an alien information virus; equally he cannot readily dismiss the theory as mere paranoia. He thinks Burroughs is onto something real and important and that his statements do far more good than harm — and he separates the two things that can be judged separately, the statement of the problem, which is correct, from the analysis of its cause, which may be faulty.
mention_cards.pith: he states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty; still, merely to be aware of the problem is to achieve a great deal
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Perhaps, then, the selfmonitoring circuit is itself malfunctioning. I cannot accept Burroughs’ view that we have been invaded by an alien virus, an information virus, yet on the other hand I cannot readily dismiss this bizarre theory as mere paranoia on his part. I think he is onto something real and impor­ tant, and that his statements do more good—far more good— than harm (that is, he states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty; still, merely to be aware of the problem is to achieve a great deal). Now, I have been able to find accounts in ancient times of what seems to be _a_ …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Later in the same letter, and this is where the disagreement is named and bounded. Dick has been assembling ancient evidence for a universal occlusion — accounts of Adam deprived of his bright nature and becoming dark, of the first humans able to see distant objects and now able to see only what is near, and the passage from Calvin he quotes in the tractate at the end of VALIS. His argument from that material is chronological: if you grant an occlusion at all, it is of long standing, and world mythology supports this, not only the Christian kind. So Burroughs may indeed have detected an information virus, or something like one, without the invasion his theory requires. The disagreement is then reduced to one question of valence, with the conditional doubled for emphasis: if an information life form exists — a bizarre and wild supposition — it is benign, it does not occlude us, and on the contrary it informs us. The parenthesis offers a third possibility he does not pursue, that it has no interest in either and simply rides our own information traffic, using our media as a carrier.
mention_cards.pith: it is benign; it does not occlude us; on the contrary: it informs us
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Burroughs may have indeed detected an “information virus” or something like an information virus, but my supposition is that, if you grant its existence, it is of long-standing. World mythology supports this. Not just Christian. Where Burroughs and I sharply disagree is that my supposition is that if— if—an information life form exists (and this is indeed a bizarre and wild sup­ position), it is benign; it does not occlude us; on the contrary: it informs us (or perhaps it has no interest in doing either, but simply rides our own information traffic, using our media as a carrier; that is entirely possible). That I myself saw this living information in the spring of 1974 is not something I wish to claim; on the other hand, I will not deny it. The issue is …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982, p. 146
mention_cards.context: The close of the Brig Elliot letter, and the sharpest thing in the dossier. Dick has just said that he will neither claim nor deny having seen this living information in the spring of 1974, and he calls the issue important, vital and elusive. Then he turns the hypothesis on the person holding it. If you grant an occluding information virus, are you not then yourself occluded in your very analysis of it, and in your perception that it exists at all? He names the difficulty as a paradox, tells his correspondent he is sure he can see it, and says that he tries to deal with it in VALIS. He does not resolve it in the letter. The remainder turns to books Elliot had recommended — Flann O'Brien's The Third Policeman, which he has not yet read, and The Tibetan Book of the Dead, which he has — and to the impossibility of going into much detail in a letter.
mention_cards.pith: if you grant an occluding information virus, are you not then yourself occluded in your very analysis of it, as well as your perception of its existence? There is a paradox involved. I’m sure you can see that. And I try to deal with it in VALIS.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: The close of the letter, and the sharpest thing in the dossier: if the occlusion is real then any analysis of it is also occluded, including this one. Dick names VALIS as where he tries to deal with the trap.
mention_cards.passage: … That I myself saw this living information in the spring of 1974 is not something I wish to claim; on the other hand, I will not deny it. The issue is important, vital and also elusive; if you grant an occluding information virus, are you not then yourself occluded in your very analysis of it, as well as your perception of its existence? There is a paradox involved. I’m sure you can see that. And I try to deal with it in VALIS. As to other matters; thank you for recommending the several books. THE THIRD POLICEMAN has …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, August 18, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Four months after the Brig Elliot exchange, writing to Patricia Warrick, Dick reaches the formulation he keeps. He describes an information life form living and doing business around us, guiding and controlling the evolution of the universe, and notes that it is primarily verbal, expressing itself as language. He then corrects his own novel. VALIS says the universe consists of information; what he should have said, he decides, is that if you roll the substantial universe back to its ontological source you find information, the Word or Torah, which shows up visibly here as Scripture but exists latently — invisible to us — everywhere. On that basis the disagreement with Burroughs is no longer about the creature's temperament but about its position: this life form has not invaded our universe, as Burroughs supposes, but is its source, one level higher, and is available to us the way the Forms are, known intelligibly rather than empirically. The letter then builds his own scheme on top of it — the Old and New Testaments as two psyches functioning as one organism in a push-pull relation, producing a third entity he calls Ditheon.
mention_cards.pith: This life form has not invaded our universe (as William Burroughs supposes) but is the source of our universe, one level higher
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … Much mention of this is made in VALIS, if you recall (viz: “the universe consists of information.” What I should have said is, “If you roll back the substantial universe to its ontological source, you will find information, the Word or Torah, which shows up here visibly as Scripture, but exists in latent—that is, invisible to us—form ubiqui­ tously”) . This life form has not invaded our universe (as William Burroughs supposes) but is the source of our universe, one level higher; it is available to us as the Forms are through a meta-abstraction on our part; that is, it is know intelligibly, rather than empirically (sensibly). So my Type A Psyche is the O.T., my Type B Psyche is the N.T., and because these two testaments function as a single organism in a push-pull dialectic relation­ ship (superimposed) they form one new, higher, third entity which I call …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, August 18, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: The last dated Burroughs reference in the archive, at the close of the same letter to Patricia Warrick. Dick sets out an ontological sequence he attributes to Erigena — God, then Logos or information, then the spatiotemporal universe, and then back to God as the goal of the whole process. He then describes what he says he did in March 1974: by means of his meta-abstraction he rolled the physical universe back to the Uttered Word underlying it, from which it derives, which is why he concludes that word is in fact an excellent translation of Logos. The image he gives is of God speaking, or rather thinking, a complex idea, from which living idea the universe came into being. And then the measurement of distance, with an exclamation mark: this view is a far cry from Burroughs's notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid. The same passage appears in the Exegesis at folio 91:19, so letter and notebook are here demonstrably one text.
mention_cards.pith: This view is a far cry from Burroughs’ notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid!
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: The last dated Burroughs reference in the archive.
mention_cards.passage: … In March, 1974, by means of my meta-abstraction I so-to-speak rolled back the physical universe to the Uttered Word underlying it, from which it is derived; this is why, finally the term “word” is in fact an excellent translation of “Logos.” It is as if God spoke (or rather thought) a complex idea, and from this living idea (Logos) the universe came into being, was derived. This view is a far cry from Burroughs’ notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid!

mention_cards.citation: Gregg Rickman, Philip K. Dick: In His Own Words — interview
mention_cards.context: The only interview in the archive where Dick discusses the word virus, and the tone is entirely unlike the notebooks: relaxed, and faintly amused. He is talking to Gregg Rickman about G. K. Chesterton's The Man Who Was Thursday, which Rickman calls a real Phil Dick reality trip because everyone turns out to belong to the same conspiracy. Dick agrees it is a lot of fun, says he knows Robert Anton Wilson and that they both love conspiracy — but not in the manner of the normal conspiracy buff, who is convinced there are demonic and malignant conspiracies to enslave mankind. His example of that kind is Burroughs's conviction about the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid, and which has taken over the planet. His verdict on it is two words: that's cool. He and Wilson, by contrast, believe in benign conspiracies, and he notes what interests him psychologically — that the dynamism behind belief in an evil conspiracy is easy to see and paranoid, whereas it is very hard to work out what is going on in someone who loves the idea of a world secretly ruled by benign people promoting health, happiness and prosperity. His answer to his own question is one word: naivety.
mention_cards.pith: the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid. They’ve taken over the planet. That’s cool.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The only interview in the archive where Dick discusses the word virus. He classes it as a malign-conspiracy belief and contrasts it with the benign conspiracy he and Robert Anton Wilson prefer — consistent with the 1981 letters, and a third venue for the same argument.
mention_cards.passage: … **GR:** That’s a real Phil Dick reality trip — everyone turns out to be a member of the same conspiracy. **PKD;** That’s a lot of fun. I know Robert Anton Wilson, and we both love conspiracy. We don’t love it in the sense of — the normal conspiracy buff, who’s convinced that there’s all these demonic and malignant conspiracies to enslave mankind. An example is (William S.) Burroughs’ convic­ tion about the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid. They’ve taken over the planet. That’s cool. Bob Wilson and I have this conviction that there are benign conspiraces going on, which is kind of interesting psychologically. You can see the psychological dynamism going on, in the conviction of an evil conspiracy, a paranoid thing. But it’s very hard to figure out what’s going on if you love the idea that the world is secretly ruled by very benign people, who are promoting health, happiness, and prosperity for …

mention_cards.citation: PKD, "How to Build a Universe That Doesn’t Fall Apart Two Days Later" (1978)
mention_cards.context: From the essay Dick wrote and delivered as a speech in 1978, the one in which he defines reality as that which, when you stop believing in it, does not go away. The surrounding argument is about manufactured worlds: we live in a society where spurious realities are produced by media, governments, corporations and religious and political groups, and the electronic hardware exists to deliver these pseudo-worlds directly into the heads of readers, viewers and listeners. He worries about what his eleven-year-old daughter is being taught by television, and about miscuing — a programme made for adults, watched by a child, half or perhaps all of it misunderstood. Into that argument comes the sentence this card exists for: the basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words, and if you can control the meaning of words you can control the people who must use them. The authority he names for it is George Orwell and Nineteen Eighty-Four, not Burroughs. He then adds the second method, controlling perception rather than language, because comprehension follows perception — which is why he thinks television's power over young minds is so vast, words and pictures being synchronised.
mention_cards.pith: The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words. If you can control the meaning of words, you can control the people who must use the words.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick’s clearest statement of language-as-control, written the same year as "William Burroughs is correct" — but he credits Orwell, not Burroughs. Lapoujade reads this passage as proximity to Burroughs (register C); Dick’s own attribution is register A. Do not collapse the two.
mention_cards.passage: … and only later on realize it. The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words. If you can control the meaning of words, you can control the people who must use the words. George Orwell made this clear in his novel _1984_ . But another way to control the minds of people is to control their perceptions. If you can get them to see the world as you do, they will think as you do. Comprehension follows perception. How do you get them to see the reality you see? After all, it is only one reality out of many. Images are a basic constituent: pictures. This is why the power of TV to influence young minds is so staggeringly vast. Words and pictures are synchronized. The possibility of total control …

mention_cards.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)
mention_cards.context: The single most useful paragraph of biography in the dossier. Sutin is describing K. W. Jeter's role after the two men resumed their friendship in late 1976, following a three-year break that began when Dick suspected Jeter might be a government agent. A former antiwar activist in the Socialist Workers Party, Jeter was not drawn to the religious theories Dick had built out of 2-3-74, but he knew how to stoke the theoretical fires and add complexities on top of Dick's own — the gadfly role, played to perfection. It is Jeter who called attention to the similarities between Dick's novels and Burroughs's, specifically an invading alien virus occluding human faculties, with the note that for Burroughs the virus is language. He has just quoted Dick on his own purpose — that the core of his writing is not art but truth, and that his corpus is one long ratiocination about an irrational, mysterious reality which helps a certain kind of sensitive, troubled person who will not blunt their own intimations. mention_cards.context: Lapoujade's causal claim, and the most contestable thing on this page. Having established the resemblance between Dick and Burroughs on language as control, he explains it not as influence but as convergence: the proximity stems in part from their readings of Alfred Korzybski, whose work describes how the use of language blocks the creativity born of relations at the level of nonverbal experience. He sets out the mechanism — the structure of language tacitly imposes the rules of an old, bivalent, Aristotelian logic on the analogical relations of the right hemisphere — and concludes that we need to be wary of language because its logic exerts control over thought and the images it generates enclose the mind in an abstract world. He then extends the argument to machines, which on this account participate in spreading the virus. concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
mention_cards.context: Lapoujade on drugs as an instrument of control rather than of escape. The argument arrives from media and advertising, which appropriate the external world behind billboards and glowing screens and are equally interested in appropriating the internal world of the psyche — the real objective being to control brains the way drugs do, since whoever controls the transmission of information controls what gets called reality. Hence the claim about Dick: there are no soft drugs in his work, only hard drugs that attack the brain directly and take control of it, as in Burroughs. That, Lapoujade says, is why drugs become a religion in Dick, a religious experience, inverting Marx's formula that religion had been the opium of the people. His case in point is The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, where two drugs circulate, sold by two dealers described as rival divinities — the first a drug of communion in which users merge with Barbie-like dolls to escape the Martian colonies, a Host that delivers them into a standardised world controlled by the dealer.
